claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is mainly enabled by a uniform, chromium-enriched passive oxide film.
A chromium-enriched passive oxide film acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
Uniform alloying-element distributions improve passive-film quality by minimizing segregation and defect sites.
Segregation and defect sites promote localized corrosion.
Conventional stainless steel with standard chromium, nickel, and molybdenum levels can form a passive film.
Conventional stainless steels typically contain microstructural heterogeneities.
Controlled thermo-mechanical treatment can reduce chromium segregation and make chromium distribution more uniform.
More uniform chromium distribution promotes formation of a continuous, defect-minimized chromium-rich oxide layer.
A coherent and continuous chromium-enriched passive layer minimizes surface defect sites and slows corrosive attack.
Optimized alloying and processing reduce microsegregation and lattice defects.
Reduced microsegregation and lattice defects enable rapid formation of a durable passive film.
The passive film limits diffusion of corrosive agents.
The passive film reduces initiation of localized corrosion such as pitting.
Steels processed for uniform chromium distribution will have lower corrosion rates than conventionally processed steels.
Steels processed for uniform chromium distribution will have lower pitting density than conventionally processed steels.
Steels processed for uniform chromium distribution will exhibit more stable passive electrochemical behavior than conventionally processed steels.
The proposed mechanism requires steels with sufficient chromium content and processing that limits elemental segregation.
The mechanism may not apply to low-alloy steels or when corrosion is dominated by factors unrelated to passive-film quality.
The controlled study compares tailored and conventionally processed steel groups under corrosive solution, irradiation, and thermal-cycling exposures.
Failure of the tailored group to show a statistically significant improvement in corrosion rate, pitting density, and passive-film quality relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
